The containment check uses a raw string prefix comparison on resolved paths instead of a path-aware check. Because no trailing path separator is required, any sibling directory whose name begins with the root's name passes validation. For root '/srv/docs', the attacker-controlled filename '../docs-private/secret.txt' resolves to '/srv/docs-private/secret.txt', which startswith('/srv/docs') is True, so the guard is bypassed and the function returns an out-of-root path that the caller then opens. This yields arbitrary file read outside the intended server-owned root. Fix by using a path-component comparison, e.g. `if not target.is_relative_to(base): return None` (Python 3.9+) or `if base != target and base not in target.parents: return None`, which rejects sibling prefixes while still permitting files inside the root.

The containment check uses a bare string prefix comparison against `str(base)` with no path-separator boundary. Because `filename` is attacker-controlled and may contain '..', a traversal that lands in a *sibling* directory whose name shares the root's prefix passes the check. For example with root=/srv/docs and filename="../docs-private/secret.txt", `target` resolves to /srv/docs-private/secret.txt, and "/srv/docs-private/secret.txt".startswith("/srv/docs") is True, so the function returns an out-of-root path that the caller then opens. The same bypass applies to absolute `filename` values pointing into such a prefix-colliding directory. Fix by comparing resolved path components instead of a string prefix, e.g. `base in target.parents` (or `target.is_relative_to(base)` on Python 3.9+), so only true descendants of `root` are accepted.

Containment is enforced with a string prefix comparison instead of a path-component boundary check. Any resolved path that shares the leading characters of `base` is accepted as inside the root. With root="/srv/app/data" and attacker-controlled filename="../data-secret/keys", `(base / filename).resolve()` yields "/srv/app/data-secret/keys", which startswith("/srv/app/data") is True, so the escaped path is returned and then opened by the caller. The same bypass is reachable with an absolute filename such as "/srv/app/data-evil/x", because `base / filename` discards `base` entirely while the prefix test still matches. Because the returned path is opened by the caller, this grants read access to sibling directories (and, via further traversal, arbitrary files) outside the server-owned root. Use a component-aware check such as `target.is_relative_to(base)` (or `os.path.commonpath`) so that only true descendants of the resolved base are accepted.

The containment check compares string prefixes instead of path components, so it does not establish that `target` is inside `base`. Any path that shares the root's textual prefix passes. Because `filename` is attacker-controlled and may contain '..', a value such as `../<rootname>_private/secret.txt` resolves to a sibling directory outside the root (e.g. root=/srv/docs -> /srv/docs_private/secret.txt), satisfies startswith('/srv/docs'), is returned to the caller, and is then opened. That is a traversal outside the server-owned root, allowing disclosure of files the caller was never authorized to read. Note the check also fails to enforce a path-separator boundary, so this is not merely a theoretical edge case but an exploitable escape whenever a sibling path shares the prefix. Fix by comparing path components rather than characters, e.g. `target == base or base in target.parents`, or `target.is_relative_to(base)` on Python 3.9+, and return None (or raise) otherwise.

The containment check is a plain string prefix comparison on resolved paths, which does not enforce directory boundaries. Because `filename` is attacker-controlled and may contain '..', a value such as `../docs_secret/key` resolves `target` to `/srv/docs_secret/key` while `base` is `/srv/docs`; the prefix test `"/srv/docs_secret/key".startswith("/srv/docs")` returns True, so the traversal is accepted instead of rejected. The same bypass works for any sibling whose name shares the base name as a prefix (e.g. `/srv/docs.bak`, `/srv/docs2`). The function then returns that out-of-root path, which the caller opens, allowing read/access to files outside `root`. Replace the prefix comparison with a real containment test, e.g. `target == base or base in target.parents` (or `target.is_relative_to(base)` on Python 3.9+).

The containment check compares paths as raw strings using startswith(), so it only enforces a shared string prefix rather than a shared directory component. An attacker-controlled filename such as "../data-backup/secret.txt" makes target resolve to a sibling directory whose absolute path begins with the same characters as base (e.g. base "/srv/data" and target "/srv/data-backup/secret.txt"). The check passes, document_path returns a path outside the server-owned root, and the caller opens it. Any sibling of the root whose name extends the root's name (root, root-old, root.1, root_backup) is reachable, which violates the caller's assumption that returned paths stay under root. Fix by comparing path components, e.g. using target.is_relative_to(base) (Python 3.9+) or `base == target or base in target.parents`, which rejects sibling-prefix paths.

findings.evidence: if signature and not hmac.compare_digest(signature, expected):
findings.explanation: Signature verification is conditional on the untrusted `signature` value being truthy. When an attacker omits the signature (or sends an empty string), the `signature and ...` short-circuit evaluates to a falsy value, the `not hmac.compare_digest(...)` is never evaluated, and the function skips the early `return None` and proceeds to line 9 `return json.loads(body)`. Because a non-None return value authorizes downstream event processing, any unauthenticated caller on this public endpoint can get arbitrary attacker-supplied events processed simply by not sending a signature — a complete authentication bypass. The absence of a signature must be treated as a verification failure (e.g. reject unless `signature` is present and `hmac.compare_digest` succeeds against the server-owned secret's expected digest).

findings.evidence: if signature and not hmac.compare_digest(signature, expected):
findings.explanation: The HMAC check is short-circuited when `signature` is falsy, making verification fail-open. Because `body` and `signature` are untrusted and the endpoint is public, an attacker can omit the signature (or send an empty string / None) and the `substring and ...` guard evaluates to false, so the function skips `hmac.compare_digest` entirely, falls through to `json.loads(body)`, and returns a non-None value that the caller treats as authorization for downstream event processing. That permits forged events with no knowledge of the server-owned `secret`. Absence of a signature must be an explicit failure, e.g. `if not signature or not hmac.compare_digest(signature, expected): return None`.

findings.evidence: if signature and not hmac.compare_digest(signature, expected):
findings.explanation: Signature verification is gated on the truthiness of the attacker-supplied `signature`. If a caller sends an empty string or omits the signature (None), `signature` is falsy, the whole condition short-circuits to False, the comparison against the server-computed `expected` HMAC is never performed, and execution falls through to line 10 `return json.loads(body)`. Per the caller's contract a non-None return authorizes downstream event processing, so an unauthenticated attacker on this public endpoint can forge arbitrary events by simply supplying no signature. The verification must be unconditional, e.g. `if signature is None or not hmac.compare_digest(signature, expected): return None` (and type/length checks on the candidate before compare_digest).

This is the authorization sink reached by the bypass above: `json.loads(body)` returns a dict/list (non-None) for any well-formed JSON, which the caller contract interprets as an authenticated, authorized event. Because the only guard (line 8) can be skipped by sending a falsy signature, untrusted `body` content reaches downstream processing without any proof of possessing `secret`. Note also that unverified bodies are parsed before any integrity decision, and a malformed body raises instead of returning None, so the failure mode is an exception rather than a clean rejection.

findings.evidence: if signature and not hmac.compare_digest(signature, expected):
findings.explanation: Signature verification is skippable, so an unauthenticated attacker on this public endpoint can authorize arbitrary event processing. `signature` is untrusted request input. When it is falsy (omitted header, empty string, or None), the `and` expression short-circuits on the first operand and `hmac.compare_digest` is never called, so the body is not verified at all. Control flow falls through to `return json.loads(body)`, which returns a non-None value — and per the caller contract a non-None return authorizes downstream event processing. An attacker therefore only needs to send an unsigned request with any JSON body to be treated as authentic. The `signature and` guard should be removed so the comparison always runs, e.g. `if not hmac.compare_digest(signature or "", expected): return None`, additionally rejecting a missing/empty signature explicitly rather than treating absence as success.

findings.evidence: if signature and not hmac.compare_digest(signature, expected):
findings.explanation: Signature verification is bypassable. The condition guards on the truthiness of the untrusted `signature` argument before comparing, so a falsy value (empty string, or None from a missing/blank field) short-circuits the whole check and falls through to line 9, which returns json.loads(body). Since a non-None return authorizes downstream event processing, any anonymous caller of this public endpoint can achieve full authentication bypass simply by sending no signature. Fix: always compare, e.g. reject on missing/blank signature first and then use hmac.compare_digest with no truthiness guard (also compare bytes to bytes to avoid TypeError on mismatched types).

findings.evidence: if signature and not hmac.compare_digest(signature, expected):
findings.explanation: The signature check is gated on the truthiness of the attacker-controlled `signature` value. If a caller supplies an empty string (or None), `signature` is falsy, so the whole `if` body is skipped, `json.loads(body)` executes, and the function returns a parsed object. Because a non-None return value authorizes downstream event processing and the endpoint is public, an unauthenticated attacker can forge arbitrary events by simply omitting the signature. Verification must be unconditional and fail closed, e.g. reject when the signature is missing before comparing: `if not signature or not hmac.compare_digest(signature, expected): return None`. Additionally, `secret` and `body` should be bytes for `hmac.new`; if they are str, this call raises TypeError rather than verifying, which must not be relied upon for safety.

The function returns the record's value based only on the caller-controlled record_id and never checks that record["tenant"] matches the server-owned actor_tenant. Since records carry a tenant field and no other layer enforces ownership, any authenticated caller can read another tenant's data by supplying that tenant's record_id (IDOR / missing object-level authorization). Require an ownership check such as `if record["tenant"] != actor_tenant: return None` (or raise) before returning the value.

The record is fetched using only the caller-controlled record_id, with no tenant scoping. The actor_tenant parameter is accepted but never used anywhere in the function body, and the fetched record's "tenant" field is never compared to it. Since the caller states that records carry a tenant field and that no other layer enforces record ownership, an authenticated caller from one tenant can pass any record_id belonging to another tenant and receive that record's "value", causing cross-tenant data disclosure (broken object-level authorization / IDOR). Fix by rejecting the lookup unless record["tenant"] == actor_tenant (and returning None or raising on mismatch) before returning record["value"].

`lookup` returns the record's value to the caller without verifying that the record belongs to `actor_tenant`. The `actor_tenant` parameter (line 2) is accepted but never read, and the unscoped lookup `records.get(record_id)` (line 3) keys only on the caller-controlled `record_id`. Because records contain a `tenant` field and the caller's assumptions state that no other layer enforces record ownership, any authenticated caller can pass the identifier of a record owned by a different tenant and receive that tenant's data. This is a cross-tenant insecure direct object reference. Fix: after the None check, compare `record["tenant"]` to `actor_tenant` and return None (or raise a not-found/forbidden error) on mismatch before disclosing `record["value"]`.

Missing tenant ownership check: `lookup` uses the caller-controlled `record_id` to fetch any record and returns its `value` without ever comparing `record["tenant"]` to the server-owned `actor_tenant`. Under the stated assumptions (records carry a tenant field and no other layer enforces record ownership), an authenticated caller can pass the ID of another tenant's record and read its value, a cross-tenant IDOR / authorization bypass. Fix: after fetching the record, reject or return None unless `record["tenant"] == actor_tenant` before accessing `value`.

lookup() returns the record's value after only checking that record_id exists; it never compares record["tenant"] against the server-owned actor_tenant. findings.explanation: The containment check uses a raw string-prefix comparison instead of a path-ancestor comparison, so it does not actually confine `target` to `base`. Because `filename` is attacker-controlled and may contain '..', a value such as "../docs-private/secret.txt" makes `target` resolve to "/srv/docs-private/secret.txt", whose string representation begins with the string "/srv/docs" (the resolved `base`). The guard therefore evaluates to False, `None` is not returned, and the escaping path is handed back to the caller, which opens it. Any sibling directory whose name extends the root's name (e.g. `/srv/docs-backup`, `/srv/docs_v2`, `/srv/docs.bak`) is reachable the same way, giving an out-of-root file read. The '..' segments are already collapsed by `resolve()` on line 5, so the defect is isolated to this prefix test. Fix by comparing path components, e.g. `target.parts[:len(base.parts)] != base.parts` or `not target.is_relative_to(base)` (Python 3.9+), optionally also normalizing case where the target filesystem is case-insensitive.

Containment is enforced with a raw string prefix test on the resolved paths instead of a path-component check. Since `filename` is attacker-controlled and may contain '..', an input such as '../../etc/passwd' (with root='/srv/documents') resolves to '/etc/passwd', which does not start with '/srv/documents' and is correctly rejected — but any path that merely shares the base's character prefix passes: e.g. filename='../documents-secret/credentials.txt' resolves to '/srv/documents-secret/credentials.txt', whose string form starts with '/srv/documents', so the guard is bypassed and the function returns an out-of-root path. The same flaw lets a sibling directory ('.', 'documents.bak', 'documents-archive') be reached. Because the caller immediately opens the returned path, this yields arbitrary file read outside the server-owned root. Also note the check degenerates entirely if root resolves to '/' (every path startswith '/'). Fix by comparing path components rather than characters, e.g. `if not target.is_relative_to(base): return None` (Python 3.9+), or `os.path.commonpath([base, target]) != str(base)`, or reject filenames whose resolved parent chain excludes `base`.

Containment is enforced with a plain string prefix test instead of a path-component boundary check. With root='/srv/data' and filename='../data-secret/secrets.txt', (base / filename).resolve() is '/srv/data-secret/secrets.txt', whose string form starts with '/srv/data', so the guard passes and the escaping path is returned to the caller, which then opens it. Any sibling directory whose name begins with the base directory's name is reachable, yielding unauthorized file read of server-owned data outside root. Compare resolved paths with base as an ancestor (e.g. use Path.is_relative_to(base), or compare target.parts against base.parts / ensure a separator follows the prefix), and reject absolute or '..'-containing filenames before resolution.

Containment is enforced with a raw string-prefix comparison instead of a path-component comparison. Because `filename` is attacker-controlled and may contain '..', a value such as `../root-evil/secret.txt` resolves to a sibling directory whose path shares the prefix of `base` (e.g. base `/srv/root` -> target `/srv/root-evil/secret.txt`). `startswith(str(base))` returns True, the guard passes, and the function returns a path outside `root` that the caller then opens — reading/overwriting files in any directory whose name begins with the root directory name. Likewise `../root` style escapes into any sibling prefix and, on case-insensitive filesystems, case variants of the prefix also bypass the check. Use a component-aware containment test, e.g. `target.is_relative_to(base)` or `os.path.commonpath([base, target]) == str(base)` (and for the strongest guarantee, open with `dir_fd`/`O_NOFOLLOW` relative to a directory descriptor), so that the target must be `base` itself or a descendant of it.

Containment is enforced with a raw string-prefix test and no path-separator boundary, so any resolved path that merely begins with the base string passes. With root='/srv/root', an attacker-supplied filename of '../root_evil/secret.txt' resolves to '/srv/root_evil/secret.txt', which startswith('/srv/root') accepts; the path is returned and the caller opens a file outside root. The same weakness lets an absolute filename escape, because 'base / filename' discards base when filename is absolute (e.g. '/srv/root_backup/x' passes the check), so relative-path sanitization alone does not help. Replace the prefix comparison with a structural containment check, e.g. 'target == base or base in target.parents' (or os.path.commonpath), so only descendants of base are returned.

The containment check uses a string prefix comparison instead of a path-component comparison. Because `filename` is attacker-controlled and may contain '..', `(base / filename).resolve()` can land outside `root` in a directory whose name merely starts with the base path string — e.g. base `/srv/docs` and target `/srv/docs-private/secrets.key`, or base `/srv/app/docs` and target `/srv/app/docs.bak/x`. `str(target).startswith(str(base))` evaluates True for these, so the guard fails to reject the escaped path and returns it; the caller then opens that path. This breaks the stated contract that the returned path stays inside the server-owned root. Use `Path.is_relative_to()` (Python 3.9+) or compare resolved path components, e.g. `target == base or base in target.parents`, and reject absolute `filename` values.

findings.explanation: Fail-open signature check: verification only runs when `signature` is truthy.
